# AdaThinkV: Adaptive Thinking for Token-Efficient Video Reasoning

- **Authors**: Jingqi Tian, Haoji Zhang, Lin Chen, Hongbo Jin, Haonan Xu, Tianrui Zhu, Xingming Shui, Shilin Ma, Wenjing Yang, Yansong Tang
- **Venue**: cs.CV
- **Published**: 2026-08-03
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01980>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.01980v1>
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.57

## In one line

AdaThinkV trains a video multimodal LLM to decide per question whether to emit an explicit reasoning trace, by estimating from matched forced-mode rollouts whether reasoning's accuracy gain outweighs its extra tokens, and by expanding rollout groups that produce no learning signal.

## Problem

Chain-of-thought helps on hard video questions -- event ordering, state tracking, causal analysis -- but wastes decoding tokens on simple perception questions and can overcomplicate them. Existing adaptive schemes route on the confidence of a preliminary answer, which the authors argue is an indirect proxy: uncertainty does not imply further reasoning will help, and high confidence can coexist with missed temporal evidence. The quantity that actually matters is the conditional net utility of reasoning for this input -- accuracy gain minus token cost -- and it is not available as an offline difficulty label. A second, RL-side problem: on hard prompts a fixed rollout group can come back entirely unsuccessful with almost no variation in accuracy reward, so group-relative methods get no gradient, and DAPO's fix (discard the group and resample) throws away exactly the difficult-but-solvable prompts.

## Contributions

- Formulates adaptive video reasoning as prompt-level utility estimation rather than difficulty or confidence estimation, and trains mode selection without offline difficulty labels, tuned confidence thresholds or an external router.
- ThinkGain: a paired-rollout estimator of per-prompt reasoning utility that subtracts a normalised length cost from the accuracy gain between forced THINK and forced ANSWER branches on the same input, with a dead zone that abstains from supervising ambiguous prompts.
- A training design that separates marker supervision from continuation learning: forced markers are masked from the policy gradient, mode selection is trained by a supervised likelihood on the marker, and both are optimised toward the same target through different conditional factors.
- VRPO: a rollout allocation rule that keeps and progressively expands all-unsuccessful, low-dispersion groups instead of discarding them as DAPO does, recovering signal from difficult-but-solvable prompts at equal compute (27.71 vs 26.25 accuracy at ~716 GPU-hours).
- An ablation separating the two effects: ThinkGain mainly moves the accuracy-token trade-off (length down 46.6% on VRPO) while VRPO mainly raises absolute accuracy (+2.37 points).
- A unified evaluation across video reasoning, general video understanding, temporal grounding and streaming benchmarks with shared inputs, parsers and scoring rules.

## Method

The policy emits one of two formats in a single autoregressive sequence: THINK, '<think> h </think> <answer> a </answer>', or ANSWER, '<answer> a </answer>'. Only the opening tag is the mode marker; everything after it is the continuation. Training is an SFT cold start on format-balanced traces followed by RL. ThinkGain: for each prompt a fraction rho of the group's G rollouts is forced to open with <think> and the rest with <answer> -- mode identity comes from rollout position, not from parsing the text -- and the net utility is estimated as Delta(x) = mean accuracy reward under THINK minus mean under ANSWER, minus lambda times (mean THINK continuation length minus mean ANSWER length) / B. A dead zone tau converts this into a mode target: THINK if Delta > tau, ANSWER if Delta < -tau, and no target at all if |Delta| <= tau. Because the forced markers are a stratified intervention rather than on-policy actions, marker tokens are masked from the RL loss and the continuation is optimised conditional on the assigned mode; autonomous mode selection is trained separately by a supervised likelihood L_mode on the marker given the target, with the total objective L_RL + gamma L_mode. The trajectory reward adds a format term, DAPO's soft overlong penalty and a mode-consistency bonus alpha times the indicator that the sampled mode equals the target (never awarded when the target is empty). VRPO replaces DAPO's dynamic sampling: a group is retained if it has success contrast (max s_i - min s_i = 1) or accuracy-reward dispersion above delta_acc; it is expanded -- keeping the existing trajectories and the balanced mode ratio, adding four rollouts per mode -- only when every response is unsuccessful and dispersion is still below the threshold; it is discarded when the group-size cap is reached. ThinkGain is recomputed over the whole expanded group. For continuous rewards such as temporal IoU, binary success uses a fixed task threshold rather than a tuned one. Optimisation follows DAPO's clipped objective with asymmetric bounds and token-level aggregation normalised across the prompt, so recovered larger groups do not dominate the minibatch; no KL penalty or reference model. At inference the forcing is removed and the marker is generated autoregressively.

## Results

Backbone Qwen3-VL-8B; SFT cold start on 10,186 traces and RL on 30,495 prompt-only inputs spanning image reasoning, temporal grounding, text reasoning and video QA; 16 H100s; rho = 0.5, lambda = 0.1, B = 512, tau = 0.05, alpha = 0.3, gamma = 0.1; VRPO from G0 = 8 to Gmax = 32 with delta_acc = 0.05 and task threshold 0.5; clipping 0.20/0.28. On the six-setting video reasoning suite (VideoReasonBench, VideoMathQA and its multiple-choice split, MMR-VBench with and without CoT, SciVideoBench) AdaThinkV averages 40.79 accuracy at 257.20 output tokens against VideoAuto-R1-Qwen3 at 37.81 / 332.93 -- +2.98 points with 22.7% fewer tokens, paired-bootstrap 95% CI [2.21, 3.75] -- and against Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking at 37.13 / 6,184.98, i.e. +3.66 points with 95.8% fewer tokens. Removing VRPO gives 38.32 at 235.73 tokens. The most informative table is the inference-mode comparison over the four canonical benchmarks: forced ANSWER 31.42 at 20.50 tokens, forced THINK 34.24 at 693.95, automatic 33.53 at 257.20 with 47.2% THINK openings -- so the adaptive policy sits 0.71 points below always-thinking with a 95% CI of [-1.57, 0.15] (i.e. not distinguishable from parity) while spending 62.9% fewer tokens, and 2.11 points above always-answering. The same table for VideoAuto-R1 shows a much lower think rate (16.8%) and a worse auto point (30.03 at 370.43). Reasoning length tracks difficulty only moderately: across difficulty tertiles the think rate rises from 25.6% to 69.1% and mean THINK length from 151 to 612 tokens, with a prompt-level length-difficulty rank correlation of 0.39. Component ablation over four benchmarks: GRPO 27.45 at 612.40 tokens, SAPO 28.06 at 568.60, DAPO 28.54 at 524.25, VRPO alone 33.23 at 481.85; adding ThinkGain to DAPO gives 31.16 at 235.73 (+2.62 points, more than halving length) and to VRPO 33.53 at 257.20 (+0.30 points, length down 46.6%). So ThinkGain buys the accuracy-per-token trade and VRPO buys the absolute accuracy (+2.37 points with ThinkGain fixed). Stage ablation: RL only 35.59 accuracy, 92.4% format compliance, 660.20 tokens, 87.5% think; SFT only 36.80 / 99.1 / 260.48 / 33.9; SFT then RL 40.79 / 99.3 / 257.20 / 49.1. Training efficiency: fixed G = 8 reaches 26.00 accuracy for 494 GPU-hours and G = 32 reaches 26.87 for 1,975, while VRPO reaches 27.71 for 716 GPU-hours against a compute-matched fixed-mix control at 26.25 for 718 and an expand-everything variant at 27.01 for 765. Beyond the reasoning suite: first on four of five general video understanding benchmarks (within 0.4 points of the best Video-MME), first on all but one temporal grounding metric (Charades-STA R@0.5 75.2 / mIoU 64.0, ActivityNet 54.9 / 52.2, NExT-GQA 81.4 accuracy / 44.5 mIoU), and first on both streaming benchmarks (StreamingBench 79.79, OVO-Bench 64.02). All numbers are from GPU inference and training; there is no hardware or human study.

## Limitations

Stated in the text rather than in a limitations section: the ThinkGain target is a finite-sample Monte Carlo estimate, so it is a utility preference rather than a ground-truth difficulty label, and the dead zone suppresses small differences without giving any statistical guarantee -- the authors explicitly treat the mode supervision as noisy. VRPO reuses the same expanded group both to estimate the ThinkGain target and to compute the policy update, which can introduce optional-stopping selection bias; this is quantified only in the supplement, against an independently resampled control. Worth noticing: the headline comparison is against baselines on different backbones (VideoAuto-R1-Qwen2.5 and -Qwen3), so part of the 2.98 points is not attributable to the method; the honest efficiency claim is the inference-mode table, where automatic selection is 0.71 points *below* always-thinking with a confidence interval spanning zero -- the contribution is 62.9% fewer tokens at approximate parity, not higher accuracy than reasoning; absolute accuracy on the hardest benchmark is very low (VideoReasonBench 7.57), so the adaptive decision is being learned in a regime where the THINK branch rarely succeeds; the length-difficulty correlation of 0.39 is modest, meaning the policy's spending is only loosely aligned with need; only one backbone at one size is trained, so nothing is shown about how the reasoning-utility estimate behaves as capability changes; the RL mixture includes image and text-only data, so the video-specific contribution is not isolated; and lambda, tau and delta_acc are fixed rather than swept in the main text, while lambda directly sets the exchange rate between accuracy and tokens that the whole method optimises.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: Squarely on topic: the paper's stated question is whether explicit reasoning is worth its token cost for a given input, and its central object -- ThinkGain -- is an explicit estimator of the accuracy-per-token exchange rate, with lambda as the tunable price of a reasoning token. Three things are useful to the group beyond the framework itself. First, the argument against confidence-based routing is made concretely: uncertainty is not the same as expected benefit from further reasoning, and the paper contrasts a confidence router that exits early before localising the evidence with a utility-trained policy that reasons only until the decisive evidence is connected. Second, the inference-mode table is the cleanest form of the result the topic cares about: forced ANSWER 31.42 at 20.5 tokens, forced THINK 34.24 at 694 tokens, adaptive 33.53 at 257 tokens with 47.2% think rate -- the adaptive policy is statistically indistinguishable from always-thinking (gap 0.71, CI [-1.57, 0.15]) at 62.9% of the cost, which is a parity-at-lower-cost claim rather than an accuracy claim, and it is worth recording as such. Third, the diagnostic that the think rate rises from 25.6% to 69.1% across difficulty tertiles and mean reasoning length from 151 to 612 tokens, with a length-difficulty rank correlation of only 0.39, is direct evidence about how well a learned stopping policy actually tracks need. The VRPO half is an RL-training contribution about zero-variance groups and is only incidentally related to the topic.

## Abstract

Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can improve performance on difficult video questions but often wastes decoding tokens on simple ones. We study whether a video multimodal large language model can adapt its reasoning effort to each question. We propose AdaThinkV, an adaptive framework for video reasoning that learns whether to reason explicitly without offline difficulty labels, manually tuned confidence thresholds, or an external router. During reinforcement learning, AdaThinkV samples matched rollouts in explicit reasoning and direct answering modes for each prompt. ThinkGain estimates the prompt-level utility of explicit reasoning by balancing its accuracy gain against additional response length, providing supervision for both conditional response generation and autonomous mode selection. For difficult prompts, limited rollout exploration can yield groups in which every response is unsuccessful and accuracy rewards show little variation, providing insufficient signal for learning. We therefore introduce Variance Recovery Policy Optimization (VRPO), which retains and progressively expands these groups to recover informative signals from prompts that are difficult yet solvable. At inference, AdaThinkV selects a response mode and generates the response in a single autoregressive sequence. Across a unified suite of video reasoning evaluations, AdaThinkV achieves a mean accuracy of 40.79 with an average of 257.20 output tokens, outperforming the strongest evaluated adaptive baseline by 2.98 points while using 22.7% fewer tokens. Project page: https://trilarflagz.github.io/AdaThinkV/
